Microtubules. Rigid cylindrical polymers built from tubulin proteins, forming one of the three major components of the cell's cytoskeleton. These 25-nanometer structures organize cellular architecture, enable chromosomal segregation during cell division, and propel cilia and flagella. Among the most dynamic cellular structures, they constantly polymerize and depolymerize in response to cellular signals.

They're assembled from alternating alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin dimers, polymerized into hollow tubes with 13 protofilaments arranged in a cylinder. The microtubule lattice has polarity: the plus end grows faster, while the minus end grows slowly. This asymmetry underlies directional transport along microtubule tracks. Kinesin motors walk toward the plus end, dynein motors toward the minus end, carrying cargo-laden vesicles through the cell.

Microtubule-associated proteins like tau and MAP2 stabilize them and regulate their dynamics, with dysregulation implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. During mitosis, centrioles nucleate microtubule organizing centers that radiate spindle fibers, which grasp chromosomes and pull sister chromatids to opposite poles. Cilia and flagella are motile organelles built on a 9+2 core—nine doublet microtubules surrounding two central singlets—driven by dynein motor proteins.

Microtubule dynamics are tightly regulated by GTP hydrolysis. Beta-tubulin carries GTP, and polymerization requires GTP-bound monomers. Catastrophe and rescue events create dynamic instability, where microtubules rapidly switch between polymerization and depolymerization phases. The plus end has a characteristic cap of uncrosslinked tubulin, determining stiffness and stability during polymerization.

Taxol and other microtubule-stabilizing drugs are used in cancer chemotherapy because cancer cells rely heavily on microtubule dynamics for rapid mitotic spindle assembly. Microtubule severing proteins like katanin and spastin break microtubules into fragments, regulating cellular architecture and enabling remodeling of the cytoskeleton during cell division.
